Text: JVM threads share the common {{c1::Heap}} and {{c2::Metaspace}} memory regions.
Extra: While sharing heap memory allows threads to communicate extremely fast, it introduces data visibility issues and race conditions.

Text: Each JVM thread possesses its own private {{c1::Stack}} and {{c2::Program Counter (PC)}} register.
Extra: This isolation prevents local variable states and execution paths from being corrupted by other threads.

Text: To execute a thread asynchronously, you must invoke the {{c1::start()}} method; calling {{c2::run()}} directly executes it synchronously on the caller's stack.
Extra: `start()` requests the OS thread scheduler to allocate resources, whereas `run()` is just a standard method call.

Text: A newly created thread is in the {{c1::NEW}} state until its {{c2::start()}} method is called.
Extra: In this state, it exists only as a Java Heap object; no system resources are allocated.

Text: When a thread is waiting to acquire a monitor lock held by another thread, it is in the {{c1::BLOCKED}} state.
Extra: Once the lock is released, the thread can transition back to the `RUNNABLE` state.

Text: Calling `thread.join()` causes the calling thread to enter the {{c1::WAITING}} state until the target thread enters the {{c2::TERMINATED}} state.
Extra: Under the hood, this coordination is driven by the JVM's native wait-and-notify loop.

Text: Under the hood, `thread.join()` uses a synchronized loop on the condition {{c1::threadB.isAlive()}} inside which {{c2::wait()}} is called.
Extra: When Thread B terminates, the JVM natively calls `notifyAll()` to wake up the waiting parent thread.

Text: A static call to `Thread.sleep()` pauses execution but does **not** release {{c1::locks/monitors}} held by the thread.
Extra: If locks need to be released during a wait, `Object.wait()` should be used instead.

Text: By default, the JVM will exit when only {{c1::daemon}} threads remain alive, discarding them immediately.
Extra: User threads (non-daemon threads), such as the main thread, keep the JVM running.

Text: An operation is {{c1::atomic}} if it executes as a single, indivisible unit of work where no intermediate states are visible to other threads.
Extra: Safe concurrent counters use CPU instructions (like Compare-And-Swap) to enforce atomicity without locking overhead.

Text: The {{c1::volatile}} keyword guarantees variable {{c2::visibility}} and {{c3::ordering}}, but does not guarantee {{c4::atomicity}}.
Extra: While it ensures threads read the most recent write from main RAM, it cannot protect compound operations from race conditions.

Text: In 32-bit JVM architectures, reads/writes of {{c1::long}} and {{c2::double}} are non-atomic unless declared with the {{c3::volatile}} keyword.
Extra: Without `volatile`, these 64-bit variables can suffer from word tearing, where writes are split into two 32-bit operations.
